notes:
1. Mughal Empire — Overview

  • The Mughal Empire was founded in northern India by Babur in 1526 CE.
  • Mughal political authority lasted in different forms until 1857.
  • The period of greatest imperial power extended from Akbar to Aurangzeb.
  • Major Mughal centres included:
  • Agra.
  • Delhi.
  • Fatehpur Sikri.
  • Lahore.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mughal Empire → Founded by Babur → 1526

2. Major Mughal Emperors

The principal Mughal rulers were:

  • Babur → 1526–1530.
  • Humayun → 1530–1540 and 1555–1556.
  • Akbar → 1556–1605.
  • Jahangir → 1605–1627.
  • Shah Jahan → 1628–1658.
  • Aurangzeb → 1658–1707.
📌 TNPSC Memory Chain

Babur → Humayun → Akbar → Jahangir → Shah Jahan → Aurangzeb

3. Babur

  • Babur's full name was Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur.
  • He was born in 1483.
  • He was a descendant of:
  • Timur through his father's line.
  • Chinggis Khan through his mother's line.
📌 Must-Memorise

Babur → Timurid + Chinggisid Lineage

4. Babur's Homeland

  • Babur originally ruled Fergana in Central Asia.
  • He later captured Kabul in 1504.
  • Kabul became the main base for his Indian campaigns.
📌 Must-Memorise

Babur → Kabul → 1504

5. Meaning of Babur

  • The name Babur is traditionally associated with the word for tiger or lion in Central Asian usage.
  • More important for TNPSC is his Timurid origin and Kabul base.

6. Political Situation Before Babur

Northern India was divided among:

  • Ibrahim Lodi's Delhi Sultanate.
  • Rajput powers.
  • Afghan chiefs.
  • Regional kingdoms.

Internal conflict weakened the Lodi position.

7. First Battle of Panipat

  • The First Battle of Panipat was fought on 21 April 1526.
  • Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi.
📌 Must-Memorise

1526 → First Panipat → Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi

8. Importance of First Panipat

The battle marked:

  • End of the Lodi dynasty.
  • End of the Delhi Sultanate.
  • Beginning of Mughal rule in northern India.

9. Babur's Military Advantage

Babur effectively used:

  • Field artillery.
  • Matchlock firearms.
  • Mobile cavalry.
  • Defensive carts.
  • Tactical manoeuvres.

10. Ustad Ali Quli

  • Ustad Ali Quli was an important artillery expert in Babur's army.
  • He was associated with gun deployment at Panipat.

11. Mustafa Rumi

  • Mustafa Rumi was another Ottoman-style artillery specialist serving Babur.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Babur's Artillery → Ustad Ali Quli + Mustafa Rumi

12. Araba System

  • Babur tied carts together to create defensive barriers.
  • Openings were left for cavalry and artillery operations.

13. Tulughma

  • Tulughma was a manoeuvring tactic involving divisions of troops moving around enemy flanks.
📌 Must-Memorise

Babur → Tulughma + Artillery

14. Battle of Khanwa

  • Battle of Khanwa was fought in 1527.
  • Babur fought the Rajput confederacy led by Rana Sanga of Mewar.
  • Babur won the battle.
📌 Must-Memorise

1527 → Khanwa → Babur Defeated Rana Sanga

15. Rana Sanga

  • Rana Sanga was the powerful ruler of Mewar.
  • His full name was Rana Sangram Singh.
  • He organised a major Rajput coalition against Babur.

16. Importance of Khanwa

  • Babur's victory consolidated his position in northern India.
  • It weakened the possibility of a powerful Rajput challenge to his new empire.

17. Ghazi Title

  • After Khanwa, Babur adopted the title Ghazi.
  • It symbolised victory in warfare framed in religious terms.

18. Battle of Chanderi

  • Battle of Chanderi was fought in 1528.
  • Babur defeated Medini Rai.
📌 Must-Memorise

1528 → Chanderi → Babur vs Medini Rai

19. Battle of Ghaghra

  • Battle of Ghaghra was fought in 1529.
  • Babur defeated Afghan forces in eastern India.
📌 Must-Memorise

1529 → Ghaghra → Babur vs Afghan Chiefs

20. Babur's Major Battle Sequence

  • Panipat → 1526.
  • Khanwa → 1527.
  • Chanderi → 1528.
  • Ghaghra → 1529.
📌 TNPSC Favourite Chronology

1526 → 1527 → 1528 → 1529

21. Baburnama

  • Babur wrote his autobiography, Baburnama.
  • It was originally written in Chagatai Turkish.
📌 Must-Memorise

Baburnama → Babur → Chagatai Turkish

22. Tuzuk-i-Baburi

  • Baburnama is also known as Tuzuk-i-Baburi.
  • It contains observations on:
  • Geography.
  • Plants.
  • Animals.
  • Cities.
  • Society.
  • Political events.

23. Persian Translation of Baburnama

  • Baburnama was later translated into Persian during Akbar's reign.
  • Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan is associated with the Persian translation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Baburnama Persian Translation → Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan

24. Babur and Gardens

  • Babur introduced and patronised Central Asian-style garden traditions.
  • He favoured geometrically arranged gardens with flowing water.

25. Charbagh

  • Charbagh means a garden divided into four major sections.
  • It became an important Mughal landscape form.
📌 Must-Memorise

Charbagh → Four-Part Garden

26. Death of Babur

  • Babur died in 1530.
  • He was initially buried at Agra.
  • His remains were later transferred to Kabul.
📌 Must-Memorise

Babur's Tomb → Kabul

27. Humayun

  • Nasir-ud-din Muhammad Humayun succeeded Babur in 1530.
  • He faced:
  • Afghan resistance.
  • Rival brothers.
  • Regional rulers.
  • Administrative instability.

28. Humayun's Brothers

Important brothers included:

  • Kamran Mirza.
  • Askari Mirza.
  • Hindal Mirza.

Internal family rivalry weakened Humayun.

29. Sher Khan

  • Farid Khan emerged as the most powerful Afghan challenger to Humayun.
  • He later became known as Sher Khan and then Sher Shah Suri.

30. Battle of Chausa

  • Battle of Chausa was fought in 1539.
  • Sher Khan defeated Humayun.
📌 Must-Memorise

1539 → Chausa → Sher Shah Defeated Humayun

31. Title Sher Shah

  • After his victory, Sher Khan increasingly asserted sovereign authority as Sher Shah.

32. Battle of Kannauj / Bilgram

  • Battle of Kannauj was fought in 1540.
  • Sher Shah again defeated Humayun.
📌 Must-Memorise

1540 → Kannauj/Bilgram → Sher Shah Victory

33. Humayun's Exile

  • After defeat, Humayun lost his Indian kingdom.
  • He spent years in exile.
  • He eventually received assistance from the Safavid ruler of Persia.

34. Safavid Assistance

  • Shah Tahmasp I of Persia assisted Humayun.
  • This helped Humayun recover:
  • Kandahar.
  • Kabul.

35. Sur Interregnum

  • Mughal rule in northern India was interrupted from 1540 to 1555 by the Sur dynasty.
  • Sher Shah Suri was its most important ruler.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1540–1555 → Sur Interregnum

36. Sher Shah Suri

  • Sher Shah ruled from 1540 to 1545.
  • Although not a Mughal, his administrative reforms strongly influenced later Mughal governance.

37. Sher Shah's Original Name

  • His original name was Farid Khan.
📌 Must-Memorise

Farid Khan → Sher Shah Suri

38. Sher Khan Title

  • Tradition associates the title Sher Khan with his killing of a tiger.

39. Sher Shah's Administration

He introduced important reforms in:

  • Land revenue.
  • Roads.
  • Currency.
  • Postal communication.
  • Military administration.

40. Rupiya

  • Sher Shah issued a standard silver coin known as the rupiya.
  • It became an important ancestor of the later rupee.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sher Shah → Silver Rupiya

41. Dam

  • Copper coins called dams were also widely used.
  • Mughal monetary terminology later continued to use dam.

42. Grand Trunk Road

  • Sher Shah improved the great road linking eastern and northwestern India.
  • It connected regions from Bengal toward the Indus frontier.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sher Shah → Grand Trunk Road

43. Sarais

  • Sher Shah constructed sarais or roadside rest houses.
  • They supported:
  • Travellers.
  • Merchants.
  • Postal communication.

44. Postal System

  • Horses and messengers were stationed at sarais.
  • This improved imperial communication.

45. Sher Shah's Land Revenue

  • Land was measured.
  • Productivity and crop values were considered.
  • Cultivators received written agreements.

46. Patta

  • Patta was a written document stating:
  • Land area.
  • Revenue demand.
📌 Must-Memorise

Patta → Revenue Assessment Document

47. Qabuliyat

  • Qabuliyat was the cultivator's written acceptance of the assessed revenue.
📌 Must-Memorise

Patta + Qabuliyat → Sher Shah Revenue System

48. Sher Shah's Death

  • Sher Shah died in 1545 during the siege of Kalinjar.
  • He was killed after an accidental gunpowder explosion.

49. Sher Shah's Tomb

  • Sher Shah's tomb is at Sasaram in Bihar.
  • It stands within a large artificial tank.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sher Shah's Tomb → Sasaram

50. Humayun's Restoration

  • Weakness among later Sur rulers allowed Humayun to return.
  • Humayun recovered Delhi in 1555.
📌 Must-Memorise

Humayun Restored → 1555

51. Death of Humayun

  • Humayun died in 1556 after falling from the staircase of his library in Delhi.
📌 Must-Memorise

Humayun → Died After Falling from Library Staircase

52. Humayun's Tomb

  • Humayun's Tomb is located in Delhi.
  • It was commissioned by his widow Bega Begum, also known as Haji Begum.
📌 Must-Memorise

Humayun's Tomb → Delhi → Haji Begum

53. Architect of Humayun's Tomb

  • Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, a Persian architect, is associated with its design.

54. Importance of Humayun's Tomb

It is significant for:

  • Persian influence.
  • Charbagh planning.
  • Large-scale use of red sandstone.
  • Development of Mughal garden-tomb architecture.

55. Gulbadan Begum

  • Gulbadan Begum was Babur's daughter and Humayun's sister.
  • She wrote Humayun-nama.
📌 Must-Memorise

Humayun-nama → Gulbadan Begum

56. Akbar

  • Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar became emperor in 1556.
  • He was only about thirteen years old when he succeeded Humayun.
📌 Must-Memorise

Akbar → 1556–1605

57. Bairam Khan

  • Bairam Khan served as regent and guardian during Akbar's early reign.
  • He played a central role in defending the Mughal throne.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bairam Khan → Akbar's Regent

58. Second Battle of Panipat

  • Second Battle of Panipat was fought in 1556.
  • Mughal forces defeated Hemu.
📌 Must-Memorise

1556 → Second Panipat → Akbar's Forces vs Hemu

59. Hemu

  • Hemu was an able military commander associated with the Sur-Afghan political order.
  • He captured Delhi and assumed the title Vikramaditya before the Second Battle of Panipat.

60. Bairam Khan and Panipat

  • Mughal forces were commanded under Bairam Khan's regency.
  • The victory secured Akbar's throne.

61. End of Bairam Khan's Regency

  • Akbar ended Bairam Khan's regency in 1560.
  • Akbar then increasingly exercised personal control over administration.

62. Akbar's Expansion

Akbar expanded into:

  • Malwa.
  • Rajputana.
  • Gujarat.
  • Bengal.
  • Kashmir.
  • Sind.
  • Kabul.
  • Khandesh.
  • Parts of the Deccan.

63. Malwa

  • Malwa was conquered in 1561.
  • Its ruler Baz Bahadur was defeated.
📌 Must-Memorise

Malwa → Baz Bahadur → Akbar

64. Rani Roopmati

  • Rani Roopmati is associated with Baz Bahadur of Malwa.
  • Their story became famous in later cultural tradition.

65. Akbar and Rajputs

Akbar followed a broad policy of:

  • Alliance.
  • Matrimonial relations.
  • Appointment of Rajput nobles.
  • Military action against resistant kingdoms.

66. Amber Alliance

  • Raja Bharmal of Amber entered into alliance with Akbar.
  • His daughter married Akbar.
📌 Must-Memorise

Akbar's Early Rajput Alliance → Amber

67. Raja Bhagwan Das

  • Bhagwan Das of Amber became an important Mughal noble.

68. Raja Man Singh

  • Raja Man Singh became one of Akbar's leading commanders.
  • He held a high mansab.
📌 Must-Memorise

Raja Man Singh → Major Rajput Noble of Akbar

69. Mewar

  • Mewar under the Sisodias remained the most persistent major Rajput opponent of Akbar.

70. Siege of Chittor

  • Akbar captured Chittor in 1568.
  • The fort was a major centre of Mewar.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chittor → Captured by Akbar → 1568

71. Ranthambore

  • Akbar captured Ranthambore in 1569.

72. Maharana Pratap

  • Maharana Pratap became ruler of Mewar in 1572.
  • He resisted Mughal authority.

73. Battle of Haldighati

  • Battle of Haldighati was fought in 1576.
  • Mughal forces were led by Raja Man Singh.
  • Maharana Pratap led the Mewar forces.
📌 Must-Memorise

1576 → Haldighati → Man Singh vs Maharana Pratap

74. Haldighati — Outcome Caution

  • Mughal forces held the field after the battle.
  • Maharana Pratap escaped and continued resistance.
  • Mewar was therefore not completely subdued by the battle itself.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Haldighati ≠ End of Maharana Pratap's Resistance

75. Chetak

  • Chetak was the famous horse associated with Maharana Pratap.
  • Its story occupies an important place in Rajput tradition.

76. Gujarat Conquest

  • Akbar conquered Gujarat in 1572–1573.
  • Gujarat was economically important for:
  • Ports.
  • Overseas trade.
  • Textile production.
📌 Must-Memorise

Akbar → Gujarat → 1572–73

77. Buland Darwaza

  • Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri commemorates Akbar's Gujarat victory.
  • It is one of the monumental gateways of Mughal architecture.
📌 Must-Memorise

Buland Darwaza → Gujarat Victory → Akbar

78. Bengal

  • Mughal campaigns brought Bengal under Akbar's control during the 1570s.
  • Afghan resistance continued for some time.

79. Battle of Rajmahal

  • Battle of Rajmahal in 1576 was important in ending major Afghan resistance in Bengal.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1576 → Rajmahal → Mughal Consolidation in Bengal

80. Kashmir

  • Kashmir was incorporated into the Mughal Empire in 1586.

81. Sind

  • Mughal authority expanded into Sind during Akbar's reign.

82. Kandahar

  • Kandahar was a strategically important frontier city linking India with Iran and Central Asia.
  • Control shifted between the Mughals and Safavids at different times.

83. Akbar's Deccan Policy

Akbar turned increasingly toward the Deccan late in his reign.

Important states included:

  • Ahmadnagar.
  • Bijapur.
  • Golconda.
  • Khandesh.

84. Ahmadnagar

  • Ahmadnagar was ruled by the Nizam Shahi dynasty.
  • Mughal forces attacked it during Akbar's reign.

85. Chand Bibi

  • Chand Bibi heroically defended Ahmadnagar against Mughal forces.
  • She became famous for her resistance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chand Bibi → Ahmadnagar

86. Khandesh

  • Khandesh was annexed by Akbar.
  • Asirgarh was captured around 1601.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Asirgarh → Akbar's Deccan Expansion

87. Akbar's Administration

Akbar reorganised:

  • Central administration.
  • Provincial administration.
  • Mansabdari.
  • Revenue system.
  • Military organisation.

88. Mansabdari System

  • Mansab means rank or position.
  • Mansabdars were imperial officers assigned numerical ranks.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mansab → Rank

89. Zat

  • Zat indicated the personal rank and status of a mansabdar.
  • It influenced:
  • Salary.
  • Position at court.
📌 Must-Memorise

Zat → Personal Rank

90. Sawar

  • Sawar indicated the number of cavalrymen a mansabdar was expected to maintain, subject to imperial regulations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sawar → Cavalry Obligation

91. Zat vs Sawar

  • Zat → Personal status.
  • Sawar → Cavalry responsibility.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite Trap

Zat ≠ Sawar

92. Mansabdars

Mansabdars could include:

  • Turanis.
  • Iranis.
  • Rajputs.
  • Indian Muslims.
  • Afghans.
  • Deccanis.

This helped create a multi-ethnic imperial elite.

93. Jagir

  • A jagir was a revenue assignment given to an official in lieu of or toward salary.
  • The jagirdar did not normally own the land itself.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jagir → Revenue Assignment

94. Jagirdar

  • A jagirdar received the right to collect assigned revenue.
  • Jagirs could be transferred.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Jagirdar ≠ Absolute Landowner

95. Khalisa

  • Khalisa land was land whose revenue went directly to the imperial treasury.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khalisa → Revenue Directly to Emperor

96. Dagh System

  • Horses maintained by mansabdars were branded to prevent fraud.
  • The practice had earlier precedents under Alauddin Khalji.

97. Chehra

  • Descriptive records of soldiers helped the Mughal state verify military contingents.

98. Mir Bakhshi

  • Mir Bakhshi was responsible for:
  • Military appointments.
  • Mansab records.
  • Verification of troops.
  • Payment-related military matters.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mir Bakhshi → Military Administration

99. Wazir / Diwan

  • The chief financial official was the Diwan or Wazir.
  • He supervised:
  • Revenue.
  • Expenditure.
  • Imperial finances.
📌 Must-Memorise

Diwan → Finance

100. Mir Saman

  • Mir Saman supervised the imperial household and royal workshops.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mir Saman → Imperial Household / Karkhanas

101. Sadr-us-Sudur

  • Sadr-us-Sudur supervised:
  • Religious grants.
  • Charitable endowments.
  • Religious officials.

102. Qazi-ul-Quzat

  • Qazi-ul-Quzat was the chief judicial officer.

103. Provinces

  • Mughal provinces were called Subas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Province → Suba

104. Subahdar

  • The provincial governor was called:
  • Subahdar.
  • Sipahsalar in some contexts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Suba → Subahdar

105. Provincial Diwan

  • The provincial Diwan supervised revenue independently of the Subahdar.
  • This helped create administrative checks and balances.

106. Sarkar

  • A Suba was divided into Sarkars.

107. Faujdar

  • Faujdar maintained:
  • Law and order.
  • Military authority.
  • Security in a Sarkar or strategic region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Faujdar → Military + Law and Order

108. Pargana

  • Sarkars were divided into Parganas.
  • Parganas were important revenue units.

109. Shiqdar

  • Shiqdar performed military and law-and-order functions at the pargana level.

110. Amil

  • Amil or Amalguzar was associated with revenue collection.
📌 Must-Memorise

Amil → Revenue Collection

111. Qanungo

  • Qanungo maintained local revenue records and customary information.

112. Patwari

  • Patwari maintained village-level land and revenue records.
📌 Must-Memorise

Patwari → Village Records

113. Muqaddam

  • Muqaddam was generally the village headman.

114. Revenue Administration

Land revenue was the most important source of Mughal income.

Akbar's revenue system is especially associated with:

  • Raja Todar Mal.
📌 Must-Memorise

Akbar Revenue Reforms → Raja Todar Mal

115. Raja Todar Mal

  • Todar Mal served as a major revenue administrator under Akbar.
  • His reforms improved:
  • Measurement.
  • Classification.
  • Assessment.

116. Zabt System

  • Zabt was a system of land-revenue assessment based on:
  • Measurement.
  • Crop yields.
  • Prices.
  • Standard rates.
📌 Must-Memorise

Zabt → Measured Land Revenue System

117. Dahsala System

  • Dahsala used average produce and prices over a ten-year period to calculate revenue rates.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dahsala → Ten-Year Average

118. Dahsala and Todar Mal

  • The Dahsala system is traditionally associated with Todar Mal under Akbar.

119. Land Measurement

  • Cultivated fields were measured systematically.
  • Standard measuring instruments were used.

120. Ilahi Gaz

  • Akbar introduced a standardised gaz or measuring unit for revenue administration.

121. Polaj

  • Polaj was land cultivated regularly every year.
📌 Must-Memorise

Polaj → Regularly Cultivated

122. Parauti

  • Parauti was land temporarily left fallow to restore fertility.

123. Chachar

  • Chachar was land left uncultivated for several years.

124. Banjar

  • Banjar was land left uncultivated for a longer period.
📌 TNPSC Memory

Polaj → Regular

Parauti → Short Fallow

Chachar → Longer Fallow

Banjar → Long Uncultivated

125. Batai

  • Batai was a system in which the crop or produce was shared between cultivator and state.
📌 Must-Memorise

Batai → Crop Sharing

126. Kankut

  • Kankut estimated production using measurement and crop inspection.

127. Nasaq

  • Nasaq involved assessment based partly on previous revenue records and estimates rather than complete annual measurement.

128. Revenue in Cash

  • Mughal revenue was often assessed in cash.
  • This encouraged:
  • Market production.
  • Monetisation.
  • Commercialisation of agriculture.

129. Akbar's Religious Policy

Akbar gradually developed a policy of:

  • Tolerance.
  • Political inclusion.
  • Religious dialogue.
  • Sulh-i-kul.

130. Pilgrimage Tax

  • Akbar abolished the pilgrimage tax in 1563.
📌 Must-Memorise

1563 → Pilgrimage Tax Abolished

131. Jizya Abolished

  • Akbar abolished jizya in 1564.
📌 Must-Memorise

1564 → Jizya Abolished by Akbar

132. Ibadat Khana

  • Akbar established the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575.
  • It was used for religious discussions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ibadat Khana → 1575 → Fatehpur Sikri

133. Participants in Religious Debates

Participants eventually included scholars of:

  • Islam.
  • Hindu traditions.
  • Jainism.
  • Christianity.
  • Zoroastrianism.

134. Jesuit Missionaries

  • Jesuit missionaries from Goa visited Akbar's court.
  • They discussed Christian theology with him.

135. Mahzar

  • The Mahzar was issued in 1579.
  • It strengthened Akbar's authority in certain religious disputes among Islamic scholars.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahzar → 1579

136. Sulh-i-Kul

  • Sulh-i-kul means universal peace.
  • It promoted political tolerance toward different communities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sulh-i-Kul → Universal Peace

137. Din-i Ilahi

  • Akbar introduced an ethical fellowship commonly called Din-i Ilahi around 1582.
  • Its membership was very small.
  • It was not a mass religion.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Din-i Ilahi → Limited Elite Fellowship, Not Popular Mass Religion

138. Tauhid-i-Ilahi

  • Some historians prefer the term Tauhid-i-Ilahi for Akbar's ethical-spiritual order.

139. Fatehpur Sikri

  • Akbar developed Fatehpur Sikri near Agra.
  • It served as imperial capital for part of his reign.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fatehpur Sikri → Akbar

140. Sheikh Salim Chishti

  • Fatehpur Sikri developed near the residence of the Sufi saint Sheikh Salim Chishti.
  • Akbar deeply respected him.

141. Prince Salim

  • Akbar's son Salim, later Jahangir, was named in honour of Sheikh Salim Chishti.

142. Important Fatehpur Sikri Buildings

Important structures include:

  • Buland Darwaza.
  • Jama Masjid.
  • Tomb of Salim Chishti.
  • Panch Mahal.
  • Diwan-i-Khas.
  • Diwan-i-Am.

143. Panch Mahal

  • Panch Mahal is a five-storeyed, open-columned structure at Fatehpur Sikri.

144. Diwan-i-Am

  • Diwan-i-Am was the hall of public audience.
📌 Must-Memorise

Diwan-i-Am → Public Audience

145. Diwan-i-Khas

  • Diwan-i-Khas was used for more restricted or special audiences.
📌 Must-Memorise

Diwan-i-Khas → Private/Special Audience

146. Agra Fort

  • Akbar substantially rebuilt Agra Fort using red sandstone.
  • Later Mughal rulers added marble structures.

147. Akbar's Translation Department

  • Akbar established a translation bureau known as Maktab Khana at Fatehpur Sikri.
  • Sanskrit works were translated into Persian.
📌 Must-Memorise

Maktab Khana → Translation Bureau → Akbar

148. Razmnama

  • Razmnama was the Persian translation of the Mahabharata prepared under Akbar.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mahabharata Persian Translation → Razmnama

149. Persian Ramayana

  • The Ramayana was also translated into Persian under Akbar's patronage.

150. Abul Fazl

  • Abul Fazl was Akbar's close adviser and historian.
  • He wrote:
  • Akbarnama.
  • Ain-i-Akbari.
📌 Must-Memorise

Abul Fazl → Akbarnama + Ain-i-Akbari

151. Akbarnama

  • Akbarnama is the official history of Akbar's reign.
  • It covers:
  • Timurid ancestry.
  • Political events.
  • Imperial expansion.

152. Ain-i-Akbari

  • Ain-i-Akbari is the administrative and statistical section of Abul Fazl's work.
  • It provides information on:
  • Revenue.
  • Mansabs.
  • Provinces.
  • Army.
  • Society.
  • Crops.
  • Prices.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ain-i-Akbari → Administration of Akbar

153. Faizi

  • Faizi was Abul Fazl's brother.
  • He was a distinguished Persian poet at Akbar's court.
